name: Rigging Spire
geological_features: Forests of natural stone spires reaching up to 3 kilometers in height
Low-gravity erosion patterns creating impossibly thin rock arches
Impact-shattered terrain with sharp angular debris fields
description: Rigging Spire is a small rocky world whose low gravity has allowed erosion to sculpt the landscape into a surreal forest of towering stone needles. The spires rise kilometers above the fractured plains, their bases thick but tapering to points so fine they seem ready to snap in any wind — though the thin atmosphere provides almost none. Between the spires, fields of angular debris from ancient impacts create a treacherous terrain of sharp edges and unstable footing.

The thin atmosphere scatters what little light reaches the surface into a perpetual twilight glow, painting the stone spires in shades of rust and amber. Sound carries poorly and travels slowly, creating eerie delays in any noise that does propagate. From orbit, the spire forests cast long, parallel shadows during the low-angle dawn and dusk periods, giving the planet the appearance of a vast, bristling organism.

The spires are composed of a remarkably hard silicate-titanium composite that resists erosion far better than the surrounding rock, which is why they stand while everything around them has been worn away. Geological dating suggests the spires are the remnants of ancient volcanic intrusions, their harder magma cores left standing as the softer sedimentary layers eroded over billions of years. Some of the tallest spires contain internal crystal cavities of considerable beauty.

Rigging Spire's titanium-rich geology has attracted mining interest, though the challenging terrain makes extraction difficult even in low gravity. The spires themselves are too structurally valuable as geological records to permit demolition, and several have been claimed as navigational landmarks by pilots who use them for visual approaches to the small landing facility at the planet's equator. A modest survey station serves as base camp for geological expeditions into the deeper spire forests.
